newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian shares rise, await EU treaty accord.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian shares rise, await EU treaty accord.

text.p: Slovenian shares firmed on Wednesday and traders are pinning their hopes on further gains if parliament ratifies the EU association treaty.
Trading seen volatile over the short term.
The SBI index rose 0.99 percent or 12.84 points to 1,315.44.
"If the agreement is ratified, the index could climb by up to 30 percent over the next two to three months," one broker said.
But failure to ratify the accord may keep foreign buyers away for several months, driving the SBI index down to its December levels around 1,150, traders said.
Parliament last week postponed a vote on whether to ratify the EU association accord, which was signed in June 1996, to allow political parties more time to reach broader agreement on the issue.
"The situation tommorow could be very stormy as questions surrounding ratification of the EU association agreement could become clearer," said Davor Dubokovic, a trader at Eastbrokers.
The Constitutional Court is expected to say on Thursday whether the agreement is in line with the constitution.
Market participants said prices may also get a boost when banks open the first custodian accounts for foreigners, which is expected to happen in June.
Overall eight shares rose, eight fell and 12 were untraded. Turnover surged to 179.7 million tolars from 52.1 million.
Issue A of drug producer Lek was the most actively traded share, falling 1.51 percent to 24,150 tolars on volume of 2,503 shares for total turnover of 61.1 million tolars.
Health resort operator Terme Catez was the top gainer, jumping 4.17 percent to 12,000 tolars on volume of 25 shares on a technical rebound after last week's almost five percent tumble.
Ordinary shares of bank Dolenjska Banka led the day's decliners, falling 3.93 percent to 14,900 tolars on volume of 2,561 shares for total turnover of 40.6 million tolars.
"The fall was most probably connected to yesterday's news that the bank's shareholders delayed decision on whether to open itself to foreign shareholders," Dubokovic said.
Dolenjska bank on Tuesday decided to postpone the decision on whether to enable a 15-percent foreign ownership in the bank until the new banking law is passed.
Analysts expect the law, allowing international banks to open branches in Slovenia and to buy into local banks in line with the EU regulations, to be passed by parliament later this year.
